newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urged to reform huge "second budget".
newsitem.headline: Japan urged to reform huge "second budget".

text.p: Japan's plans to begin overhauling its debt-ridden fiscal system in 1997 will be difficult to achieve without reforming the nation's unique "second budget", analysts say.
On Tuesday, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto took heed of such calls and asked the Finance Ministry to reduce the size of the government's Fiscal Investment and Loan Programme (FILP).
The FILP is widely known as the "second budget" for the role it plays in supplementing the state budget.
Earlier this week, an influential business group also released a report calling for the FILP to be reformed to curb the government's ever-expanding fiscal spending.
The government's outstanding debt, including government bonds, totalled 334.1 trillion yen ($2.95 trillion) at the end of June.
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) forecasts that the ratio of fiscal deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) for Japan in the 1996/97 fiscal year will be 7.4 percent.
This compares with European nations which must clear a hurdle of keeping their public budget deficits under 3.0 percent of GDP to join the European Monetary Union from 1997.
"The reform of the 'second budget' is absolutely necessary to put the brakes on fiscal spending growth," the report from the Japan Federation of Economic Organisations (Keidanren) said.

The programme, which is separate from the main budget, collects funds mainly through postal savings and public pension systems and then funnels them to government agencies which make loans for public works and other projects.
It was considered one of the engines that lifted Japan out of the rubble of World War Two by systematically collecting individual's deposits and using them to develop heavy industry.
But many analysts said that role ended as Japan modernised, and that the FILP is now an obstacle on the road to streamlining government spending.
"It's about time we take a look at the FILP with its abolishment in mind," said Atsushi Miyawaki, a professor at Hokkaido University, who has written extensively on the issue.
Under the original plan for the fiscal 1996/97 year, the programme was set at 49.12 trillion yen ($434 billion). This compared with the state budget for the year of 75.10 trillion yen ($664 billion).
Keidanren said while government spending accounted for 34.5 percent of GDP in the 1994/95 fiscal year, the figure rises to 45.7 percent if FILP expenditures are included.
"We need to lower the ratio of public spending to GDP as much as possible by reforming the FILP," Keidanren said.
Analysts said reforms need to be carried out to both the "entrance" and "exit" sides of the FILP.
One major entrance is the mammoth postal savings system run by the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications.
Keidanren called for the privatisation of the system, which has long been criticised by commercial banks as taking away their business.

Postal savings deposits stood at 220.19 trillion yen ($1.94 trillion) at the end of November, while the total of deposits at Japan's 10 main commercial banks was 275.14 trillion yen ($2.43 trillion) as of the end of September.

The postal savings system provides depositors with most of the services offered by commercial banks, but the banks say they are at a disadvantage as the system is backed by the credibility of the government and offered through almost all post offices throughout Japan.
Hokkaido University's Miyawaki said that by cutting down on funding for the FILP, many of the agencies which loan out the money can either be scaled down or abolished.
Miyawaki said agencies which make housing loans to individuals should be scrapped altogether as they can be replaced by commercial financial institutions.
